docs.title: RS & GIS for Spatial Planners
docs.text:
Remote sensing and GIS with Python for architects and urban planners. Bengaluru is the case study throughout.

Planners already ask spatial questions every day. Where is green space missing? Which streets are walkable? Where is the city growing fastest? This course shows how to answer those questions with free data and short Python notebooks that run in your web browser.

docs.title: Who this is for
docs.text:
• Architects, urban designers and planners who are curious about data-driven planning
  • Students of architecture, planning and geography
  • Anyone who has used Google Maps or QGIS and wants to go one step further

You do not need to know Python. Every notebook explains each step in plain words. You run the code by pressing a button.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a lesson from the list below.
  2. Read the short lesson page to see the planning question and what you will learn.
  3. Click Open in Colab. The notebook opens in Google Colab, a free online tool, so you install nothing on your computer.
  4. Run the cells one by one and look at the maps.

New to Colab? Start with Getting Started.

docs.title: Support this project
docs.text: If this course helps you, please give it a star on GitHub. It is free and takes one click, and it helps other architects and planners find the course. You can also support it by sharing it with your colleagues and students, or by reporting a problem or suggesting a lesson.

docs.title: Learning path
docs.text:
• Lessons 1 to 5: GIS. Vector data (points, lines and polygons) from OpenStreetMap.
  • Lessons 6 to 9: remote sensing. Raster data from satellite images.
  • Lesson 10: putting it together. A suitability analysis that uses everything from the course.

Every lesson makes static maps, so you can focus on the analysis. Interactive web maps come at the end, in Lesson 10, once you are comfortable with the data. There you turn your results into a Leaflet map that anyone can open, zoom and click in a web browser.

docs.title: Bonus material
docs.text: Collecting Citizen Data with ODK and KoboToolbox is a no-code guide to field surveys. It goes from designing a phone form to putting citizen reports on a public map. Satellites and OpenStreetMap cannot tell you where garbage piles up or which footpaths are broken. Citizens can.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
Every good analysis starts with a clear research question, and the data comes second. The Data page shows how to go from a planning question to the data you need, and lists good free sources: USGS (Landsat, DEMs, CORONA), Bhoonidhi and Bhuvan for Indian satellite data, OpenStreetMap, WorldPop and more.

All data used in this course is free and open, and the notebooks download it automatically, with no account or API key needed.

docs.title: Start with your research question
docs.text:
Your research question is the most important part of any spatial analysis. It decides what data you need, for which area, from which years and at what level of detail. People often start by downloading interesting data and then look for a question to fit it. That leads to hours of downloads and a weak result.

Turn it around. Write the planning question down in one sentence first, then ask: what do I need to measure to answer it? Only then go looking for data.

Planning question What you need to measure Type of data Example source Where is green space lacking? Vegetation cover per ward Satellite image (NDVI) + ward boundaries Sentinel-2, DataMeet Which neighbourhoods are hottest? Land surface temperature Thermal satellite image Landsat 8/9 Who can walk to a park in 15 minutes? Street network, park locations Vector map data OpenStreetMap How many people lack access to a school? Population by area Population grid or census WorldPop, Census of India How has the city expanded since the 1970s? Built-up area over time Historical and recent imagery CORONA, Landsat Which areas flood after heavy rain? Elevation, low-lying land, rainfall DEM + rainfall data Copernicus DEM, CHIRPS

docs.title: Answer these before you search
docs.text:
• Where? Your exact study area: a site, a ward, a city or a region.
  • When? A single date, a season, or a change over several years.
  • How detailed? A building needs data with pixels of 1 m or less. A neighbourhood needs about 10 to 30 m, and a whole city about 100 m to 1 km.
  • How often? Is one snapshot enough, or do you need regular updates?
  • Can I use it? Check the licence, especially if you will publish the results.

Once you have these answers, here are some good places to find data.

CORONA for urban history

CORONA images show Indian cities as they were around 1965 to 1972, long before the IT boom. Comparing them with today's Sentinel-2 images is a powerful way to show urban growth, lost lakes and vanished farmland.

docs.title: Your own data
docs.text: Sometimes the data you need does not exist, for example garbage dumps, broken footpaths or streetlights that do not work. Then you collect it yourself. See the bonus guide Collecting Citizen Data with ODK and KoboToolbox.

docs.title: Before you download
docs.text:
• Licence and citation: can you share or publish the results? Who should you credit?
  • Date and season: compare like with like. For example, compare dry season with dry season in each year.
  • Cloud cover: for optical imagery, filter for scenes with little cloud.
  • Coordinate system (CRS): make sure all layers line up. Reproject if needed.
  • Detail compared with your question: 30 m pixels cannot show a single building, and street-level data may be far too much for a state-wide study.

Accounts

USGS EarthExplorer, Bhoonidhi, Bhuvan and the Copernicus Browser all need a free account. Register before your workshop or fieldwork, because approval for some products can take a day or two.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Key terms used in the course, explained for planners.

Band One layer of a satellite image, recording one colour of light (for example red, or near-infrared). A colour photo has three bands. Sentinel-2 has thirteen. Bounding box (bbox) The rectangle that encloses an area, written as four numbers: west, south, east, north. Centroid The centre point of a shape. Circuity How much longer a route along the streets is than the straight-line distance. A value of 1.0 means the streets are perfectly direct. CRS (Coordinate Reference System) The system used to give locations coordinates. Latitude and longitude (EPSG:4326) are good for storing data. A projected CRS such as UTM zone 43N (EPSG:32643) is used for measuring distances and areas in metres around Bengaluru. DEM (Digital Elevation Model) A raster where each pixel holds the ground height above sea level. Footprint The outline of a building on the ground, stored as a polygon. GeoDataFrame A table (like a spreadsheet) where each row also has a shape: a point, line or polygon. It comes from the GeoPandas package. Ground coverage The share of a plot or area covered by building footprints, in percent. Intersection density The number of street intersections per square kilometre. Higher values usually mean smaller blocks and a more walkable area. Isochrone The area you can reach from a point within a set time, for example a 15-minute walk. Land cover What physically covers the ground: trees, water, buildings, bare soil. It differs from land use, which is what people use the land for. LST (Land Surface Temperature) How hot the ground surface is, measured by a satellite's thermal sensor. On a sunny day it is often much hotter than the air temperature. NDBI (Normalised Difference Built-up Index) A satellite index that highlights built-up areas. It is calculated from short-wave infrared and near-infrared bands. NDVI (Normalised Difference Vegetation Index) A satellite index that measures how green and healthy vegetation is. It ranges from -1 to 1, and values above about 0.4 usually mean dense vegetation. Network graph A street network stored as nodes (intersections) and edges (street segments between them). OpenStreetMap (OSM) A free, editable map of the world built by volunteers, like a Wikipedia for maps. Pixel / resolution The smallest square in a raster. "10 m resolution" means each pixel covers 10 m by 10 m on the ground. Random Forest A machine learning method that learns from labelled examples and then predicts labels for new data. It works by combining many simple decision trees. Raster Data stored as a grid of pixels, like a photo. Satellite images and elevation models are rasters. Remote sensing Collecting information about the Earth from a distance, usually with satellites or drones. Slope How steep the ground is, in degrees. STAC (SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog) A standard way to search catalogues of satellite images by place, date and cloud cover. Suitability analysis Combining several map layers, each given a weight, to score how suitable every location is for a use. Vector Data stored as points, lines and polygons, for example bus stops, roads and building footprints. Zonal statistics Summarising raster values inside each zone, for example the average NDVI in each ward.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: All notebooks run in Google Colab, a free service from Google that runs Python in your web browser. All you need is a Google account.

docs.title: Opening a notebook
docs.text:
1. Go to any lesson page and click the Open in Colab button.
  2. The notebook opens in a new browser tab.
  3. If Colab asks you to sign in, use your Google account.

docs.title: Running the code
docs.text:
A notebook is made of cells. There are two kinds:

  • Text cells explain what is happening. Read these.
  • Code cells have a grey background and a play button on the left.

To run a code cell, click the play button, or click inside the cell and press Shift + Enter. Run the cells in order, from top to bottom. Each cell builds on the ones above it.

Run everything at once

The menu option Runtime > Run all runs every cell in order. This is handy if you only want to see the results.

docs.title: The first cell installs packages
docs.text:
Each notebook starts with a cell like this:

!pip install osmnx leafmap

This installs the extra tools the notebook needs. It takes about a minute, and you can ignore the long text it prints. If Colab shows a warning about restarting the session, click Restart session, then carry on from the next cell.

docs.title: Warnings in red
docs.text: You may see messages in red or pink boxes that say Warning. These are usually harmless notes from the software. An actual problem says Error and stops the cell from running.

docs.title: Saving your work
docs.text:
Colab does not save your changes to the original notebook. To keep your own version:

  • File > Save a copy in Drive saves it to your Google Drive.

docs.title: When something goes wrong
docs.text:
• A cell fails with NameError. You probably skipped a cell. Run the cells above it first.
  • Downloads are slow or time out. The data servers can be busy. Wait a minute and run the cell again.
  • OpenStreetMap downloads fail with 502, 504 or Read timed out. Lessons 1 to 5 and 10 download OSM data from the public Overpass server, which is sometimes overloaded. Wait a few minutes and try again, or switch to a mirror server by running this line after the imports: ox.settings.overpass_url = "https://overpass.kumi.systems/api"
  • Everything is stuck. Use Runtime > Restart session, then Runtime > Run all.

docs.title: Changing the study area
docs.text:
Every notebook uses Bengaluru, but you can switch to your own city. Look for the settings cell near the top:

CITY = "Bengaluru, Karnataka, India"

Change the name or the coordinates to your own city and run the notebook again. Some ward data only exists for Bengaluru, and the notebooks point out where that is the case.

docs.title: Bonus: Collecting Citizen Data with ODK and KoboToolbox
docs.text:
Planning question: How can citizens report what satellites and maps cannot see?

This bonus guide uses no Python. It shows you how to run a field survey on mobile phones and bring the results into your maps. The worked example is a citizen solid waste reporting survey in Bengaluru.

Download the full illustrated guide (PDF)

docs.title: Why citizen data matters for planners
docs.text:
Satellite images show green cover and built-up land. OpenStreetMap shows roads and buildings. But neither can tell you:

  • where garbage piles up on the street
  • which footpaths are broken or blocked
  • which streetlights are not working
  • how residents actually use a park

Citizen data, collected by residents, volunteers or students with a phone, fills these gaps. It gives you ground truth: real observations at real places. It also brings the community into the planning process.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
The guide uses four open-source tools. Each one does one job and hands the data to the next.

Tool Runs on Job KoboToolbox Web browser Design forms, then receive and review submissions ODK Collect or KoboCollect Android phone Collect data offline, with GPS and photos QGIS Desktop Clean, join, analyse and style the data Dashboard Web A Leaflet map (see Lesson 10) or a Streamlit app

ODK stands for Open Data Kit. KoboToolbox is built on it, so forms made in Kobo work in both ODK Collect and KoboCollect.

A phone form gives a field team a lot that paper cannot:

  • It works offline.
  • It adds a GPS point to every record.
  • Photos are attached to the record.
  • There are no paper sheets to re-type.

docs.title: The pipeline
docs.text:
The work always runs in this order. Start at step 1, not step 2.

  1. Plan storage
  2. Design the form
  3. Deploy
  4. Connect the phones (ODK Collect)
  5. Collect in the field
  6. Review in Kobo
  7. Archive
  8. Analyse in QGIS
  9. Build the dashboard and publish

docs.title: Step 1: Plan storage
docs.text:
Every KoboToolbox plan has a storage limit. Text submissions are tiny. Photos are what fill it up.

Do this sum before you start:

submissions you expect x photos per submission x photo size from your phones = storage you need

Take a test photo on the phones your team will use and check its file size. Compare the total with your plan's limit, and leave some headroom. Current plan limits are listed on kobotoolbox.org.

To shrink photos before they upload, add this setting to the photo question's parameters column:

max-pixels=1024

It caps the longest side of each photo at 1,024 pixels. With photos resized like this, a 1 GB plan goes a long way.

Do the maths before fieldwork, not during it

If you go over the limit anyway, archive and clear old data (see Step 7) or buy more storage from Kobo.

docs.title: Step 2: Design the form
docs.text: Start with the drag-and-drop Formbuilder in KoboToolbox. Once your form has more than about a dozen questions, switch to XLSForm: a spreadsheet where one row is one question. It is easier to version, share and fix in bulk.

docs.title: Sample form: solid waste reporting in Bengaluru
docs.text:
survey sheet

type name label relevant parameters start start end end today today select_one yesno consent Data will be published openly. Continue? select_one_from_file sites.csv site_id Which site are you at? ${consent} = 'yes' geopoint location Stand at the site ${consent} = 'yes' select_one yesno solid_waste Is there solid waste? ${consent} = 'yes' image photo Photo of the site ${solid_waste} = 'yes' max-pixels=1024

choices sheet

list_name name label yesno yes Yes yesno no No

sites.csv is a small file that you upload to the form as a media file. It holds a list of survey sites, with name and label columns, for example one row per ward from Lesson 1.

docs.title: Form design tips
docs.text:
• Geo questions: geopoint records a point, geotrace a line and geoshape a polygon. Start with points.
  • Skip logic: the relevant column hides a question until a condition is met. In the form above, nothing is asked unless the person gives consent, and the photo is only asked for when there is waste.
  • Clean names: keep the name column short, lowercase and with underscores. These names become the column headers in QGIS and your dashboard.
  • Keep start, end and today: the timestamps expose rushed or duplicate submissions.

docs.title: Steps 3 and 4: Deploy and connect the phones
docs.text:
When you sign up, Kobo asks you to pick a server: Global or EU. This decides where your data is stored. Note which one you chose, because every phone must point to it.

Deploy makes the form live. After every edit, Redeploy, then update the form on every phone.

In ODK Collect or KoboCollect:

  1. Choose Configure server manually, or go to Settings > Project Management > Server.
  2. Paste the server URL from your project, found under Form > Collect data. It looks like https://kc.kobotoolbox.org/your_username. The EU server has a different URL, so always copy it from your own project.
  3. Sign in with a dedicated data collection account, or allow anonymous submissions. Never share your main login.
  4. Download the form and send one test submission from home.

docs.title: Step 5: Collect in the field
docs.text:
Brief volunteers on four things:

  • Stand at the site. The GPS records where you are. Save once the accuracy drops below 5 to 10 m.
  • Finalise each form. Don't leave it as a draft.
  • Tap Send once you are back on a network.
  • Charge the phone before going out.

Walk the route once with a test form before the team goes out.

Once the form is live, never rename a question

You can add questions mid-collection. Renaming or deleting old ones splits your data into mismatched columns.

docs.title: Steps 6 and 7: Review, then archive
docs.text:
Use Kobo's Map view as a quick GPS check. Mark each record Approved, Not approved or On hold. That status travels into every export, so the dashboard can show approved records only.

Export two bundles:

  • GeoJSON export: geometry and attributes in one open file, which loads straight into QGIS. Keep a CSV too.
  • Media ZIP: the photo files. The photo column holds each file name, so they match up.

Deleted submissions and photos cannot be recovered from Kobo

Verify, then delete:

  1. The record count in the export matches Kobo.
  2. The photos in the ZIP match the non-empty photo values.
  3. A random handful of records show the right photo.
  4. You have two copies in two places, such as a local drive and the cloud.

Or skip deleting altogether: Kobo sells monthly storage plans.

docs.title: Steps 8 and 9: Analyse and publish
docs.text:
Drag the GeoJSON or CSV onto the QGIS map. Then:

  • Join the collected points to your base layer by a shared ID, for example the BBMP wards from Lesson 1
  • Summarise conditions per site or ward, for example the number of waste reports per ward
  • Overlay a DEM to see which problems sit in low-lying ground (see the elevation data in Lesson 10)
  • Flag poor GPS precision and records marked Not approved

Keep the archive untouched, and work on copies. Use the right format for each job:

Use Format QGIS analysis GeoPackage: geometry, attributes and styles in one file Dashboard GeoJSON for Leaflet, GeoParquet for faster Python Web photos Resized JPGs Open data CSV + GeoJSON + the XLSForm as a data dictionary, with personal information removed

Build the dashboard in this order: sketch charts in Colab, set the KPIs (decide what to measure), then build it.

  • Leaflet: a public map of finished data. One HTML file, with free hosting. Lesson 10 shows you how to make one.
  • Streamlit: filters, charts, or live data from the Kobo API.

docs.title: Privacy and consent
docs.text:
Citizen data is about people and their neighbourhoods. Before you publish:

  • Ask for consent at the start of the form, and say clearly that the data will be published.
  • Remove personal information, such as names, phone numbers and faces in photos.
  • Think about whether exact locations could identify a household. If they could, publish ward summaries instead of points.

docs.title: If you remember two things
docs.text:
1. Plan storage before the form. Resize photos to 1,024 pixels.
  2. Archive before you delete. GeoJSON plus the media ZIP, verified, in two places.

Everything else in the pipeline can be fixed later. These two can't.

docs.title: The full guide
docs.text: Guide: "From Field Data Collection to Public Dashboard" by Sonia Das.

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text:
Ten hands-on notebooks. Each one starts from a planning question and ends with a map or chart that answers it.

You can do the lessons in any order, because every notebook downloads its own data. For complete beginners, though, going in order works best.

docs.title: Part 1: GIS with OpenStreetMap
docs.text:
1. Your Study Area: city boundary, wards and your first maps
  2. Mapping the City from OpenStreetMap: buildings, roads, parks and amenities
  3. Street Network Analysis: intersection density, connectivity and street orientation
  4. The 15-Minute City: walking access to parks and schools
  5. Urban Form and Buildings: footprints, ground coverage and building shapes

docs.title: Part 2: Remote sensing with satellite images
docs.text:
1. Satellite Imagery Basics: finding and viewing Sentinel-2 images
  2. Green Cover and Built-up Areas: NDVI and NDBI by ward
  3. Urban Heat Island: land surface temperature from Landsat
  4. Urban Growth with Machine Learning: land cover classification and change over time

docs.title: Part 3: Bringing it together
docs.text: 1. Site Suitability (Capstone): where to put a new park, shared as an interactive web map

docs.title: Bonus material
docs.text: • Collecting Citizen Data with ODK and KoboToolbox: a no-code guide that takes you from a phone survey to a public map

docs.title: Lesson 1: Your Study Area
docs.text:
Planning question: What is my study area?

View on GitHub

Every planning project starts with a clear boundary. You will download the official Bengaluru boundary, measure its area, load the BBMP ward boundaries and make your first maps.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Load a city boundary from OpenStreetMap with one line of code
  • Reproject data to metres to measure areas correctly
  • Read open ward data straight from the web
  • Make a choropleth map
  • Save layers as a GeoPackage for QGIS

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• GeoDataFrame: a table where each row has a shape
  • CRS: latitude and longitude for storing, UTM (metres) for measuring
  • Choropleth map: areas coloured by a value

docs.title: What you will make
docs.text:
A map of the city boundary, and a map of the BBMP wards coloured by size.

Packages geopandas, osmnx, matplotlib Data OpenStreetMap, DataMeet BBMP wards Time 30 to 45 minutes

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
The end of the notebook includes these exercises:

  1. Compare the area of Bengaluru with Mysuru.
  2. Find the smallest ward.
  3. Try a different colour scale for the ward map.

Enjoying the course? Support it with a star on GitHub.

All lessons | Next: Lesson 2

docs.title: Lesson 2: Mapping the City from OpenStreetMap
docs.text:
Planning question: What exists on the ground?

View on GitHub

Before planning anything new, you need a base map of what is already there. You will download buildings, streets, parks and amenities for Indiranagar and combine them into a layered map.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Download any OSM layer by its tags
  • Turn polygons into points with centroids
  • Build a layered figure-ground map
  • Do a quick open-space-per-person check
  • Save all layers to one GeoPackage

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Tags: OSM describes features with key=value pairs, such as leisure=park
  • Layers: maps are built from the bottom up
  • Data quality: OSM is free but uneven, so always check it

docs.title: What you will make
docs.text:
A figure-ground map of Indiranagar showing buildings, streets, parks and amenities.

Packages osmnx, geopandas, matplotlib Data OpenStreetMap Time 30 to 45 minutes

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
The end of the notebook includes these exercises:

  1. Compare Jayanagar with Indiranagar.
  2. Add bus stations or libraries.
  3. Add water bodies with natural=water.

Enjoying the course? Support it with a star on GitHub.

Previous: Lesson 1 | Next: Lesson 3

docs.title: Lesson 3: Street Network Analysis
docs.text:
Planning question: How connected and walkable are the streets?

View on GitHub

Street patterns shape how people move. You will compare the planned grid of Jayanagar with the organic old market area of Chickpet, using standard measures of network form.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Download a street network as a graph of nodes and edges
  • Calculate intersection density, street density, dead ends and circuity
  • Map junctions and dead ends
  • Compare street orientation with polar histograms

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Graph: nodes (intersections) and edges (street segments)
  • Intersection density: more junctions usually mean better walkability
  • Orientation entropy: how ordered or grid-like a street pattern is

docs.title: What you will make
docs.text:
Side-by-side street maps, a comparison table and street orientation roses for the two areas.

Packages osmnx, networkx, pandas Data OpenStreetMap Time 30 to 45 minutes

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
The end of the notebook includes these exercises:

  1. Add a newer suburb such as Whitefield.
  2. Switch to the drive network.
  3. Test a larger study area.

Enjoying the course? Support it with a star on GitHub.

docs.title: Lesson 4: The 15-Minute City
docs.text:
Planning question: Who can walk to a park or school within 15 minutes?

View on GitHub

The 15-minute city puts daily needs within a short walk. You will measure real walking times along the street network in Koramangala, draw isochrones and map the access gaps for parks and schools.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Add walking time to every street segment
  • Draw 5, 10 and 15-minute isochrones
  • Calculate the walk from every intersection to the nearest park or school
  • Map access gaps and work out a simple 15-minute score

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Isochrone: the area reachable within a set time
  • Network distance compared with straight-line distance
  • Access gap: places beyond the target walking time

Maps of walking time to the nearest park and school, with red areas showing access gaps.

docs.title: Lesson 5: Urban Form and Buildings
docs.text:
Planning question: How dense is the urban fabric, and what shape is it?

View on GitHub

Building footprints reveal the character of a place. You will compare Jayanagar and Shivajinagar with figure-ground maps, building shape measures and a ground coverage grid.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Make figure-ground maps from OSM footprints
  • Measure footprint area, compactness, elongation and orientation with momepy
  • Calculate ground coverage on a 100 m grid
  • Compare the morphology of two neighbourhoods

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Urban morphology: the study of the form of a city
  • Ground coverage: the share of land covered by buildings
  • Shape indices: numbers that describe building form

docs.title: What you will make
docs.text:
Figure-ground maps and ground coverage heat maps for the two areas.

Packages osmnx, momepy, geopandas Data OpenStreetMap Time 30 to 45 minutes

docs.title: Lesson 6: Satellite Imagery Basics
docs.text:
Planning question: What does the city look like from space?

View on GitHub

Free satellite images show any city as it is today. You will search the Sentinel-2 catalogue, choose a cloud-free image of central Bengaluru, make true and false colour images, and compare the spectral signatures of water, trees and buildings.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Search a STAC catalogue by place, date and cloud cover
  • Load satellite bands as an xarray dataset
  • Convert raw values to reflectance
  • Make true colour and false colour composites
  • Plot spectral signatures

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Bands: each records one colour of light
  • Reflectance: the share of sunlight bounced back
  • False colour: showing invisible light, such as near-infrared, to reveal vegetation

docs.title: What you will make
docs.text:
True colour and false colour images of central Bengaluru, and a spectral signature chart.

Packages pystac-client, odc-stac, rioxarray Data Sentinel-2 L2A (Microsoft Planetary Computer) Time 30 to 45 minutes

docs.title: Lesson 7: Green Cover and Built-up Areas
docs.text:
Planning question: Where is green space lacking?

View on GitHub

Bengaluru, the Garden City, has lost much of its tree cover. You will calculate NDVI and NDBI from Sentinel-2, mask out clouds and summarise green cover for every BBMP ward.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Mask clouds with the scene classification layer
  • Calculate NDVI and NDBI
  • Rasterize wards and calculate zonal statistics
  • Rank the wards by green cover

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• NDVI: a vegetation index from -1 to 1
  • NDBI: a built-up index
  • Zonal statistics: summarising pixels within each area

docs.title: What you will make
docs.text:
A ward map of dense green cover, and a list of the least green wards.

docs.title: Lesson 8: Urban Heat Island
docs.text:
Planning question: Which neighbourhoods are hottest?

View on GitHub

Concrete and asphalt make cities hotter than their surroundings. You will map land surface temperature from Landsat's thermal band, find hot spots and the hottest wards, and measure how much cooler green areas are.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Load a Landsat thermal band and convert it to degrees Celsius
  • Mask clouds with the quality band
  • Measure heat island intensity and map hot spots
  • Calculate the mean temperature per ward and its link to NDVI

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• LST: land surface temperature, not air temperature
  • Urban heat island: built-up areas are hotter than green areas
  • Hot spot: much hotter than the city average

docs.title: What you will make
docs.text:
A land surface temperature map of Bengaluru and a ward ranking by temperature.

docs.title: Lesson 9: Urban Growth with Machine Learning
docs.text:
Planning question: How has the city expanded?

View on GitHub

East Bengaluru has grown rapidly along its IT corridors. You will train a Random Forest classifier with ESA WorldCover labels, map land cover in 2019 and 2024, and measure the new built-up area.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Turn satellite images into a table of pixels and features
  • Train and test a Random Forest classifier
  • Read precision, recall and the confusion matrix
  • Classify two years and map the change

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Supervised classification: learning from labelled examples
  • Training and test sets: checking the model on unseen data
  • Change detection: comparing classified maps over time

docs.title: What you will make
docs.text:
Land cover maps for 2019 and 2024, and a map of new built-up areas.

docs.title: Lesson 10: Site Suitability (Capstone)
docs.text:
Planning question: Where should a new park go?

View on GitHub

The capstone has two parts. In Part 1 you combine everything from the course: four criteria layers (heat, green need, flatness and road access), limited to open land and combined with weights, to shortlist the 10 best park sites in south-east Bengaluru. In Part 2 you meet interactive web maps for the first time, and turn the results into a Leaflet map that anyone can open, zoom and click in a web browser.

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
• Put satellite, elevation, land cover and OSM data onto one common grid
  • Calculate slope and distance to roads with xarray-spatial
  • Rescale criteria to 0 to 1 and apply weights
  • Shortlist the top sites
  • Build an interactive Leaflet web map with folium: basemaps, a raster overlay, layers, tooltips and popups
  • Save the web map as a single HTML file and publish it

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Multi-criteria analysis: combining weighted factors
  • Constraints compared with criteria: excluded land compared with scored land
  • Sensitivity: how results change with the weights
  • Web map: tiles, layers, tooltips and popups in Leaflet

docs.title: What you will make
docs.text:
A suitability map, and an interactive web map of the 10 candidate park sites that you can share as a single HTML file.

Packages xarray-spatial, odc-stac, osmnx, folium Data Landsat, Copernicus DEM, ESA WorldCover, OpenStreetMap Time 30 to 45 minutes
